tweets.text:
MiniMax M3.1 Flash, on more of your hardware.

Quantizing a 428B model opens up more ways to run it locally. Lower-bit weights reduce the memory needed to load the model and the weight data moved during decoding. Making those savings useful takes careful calibration, efficient low-bit kernels, and hardware-aware placement of experts across GPU and system RAM.

Thank you to the builders doing that work:

• @UnslothAI @danielhanchen — 2-bit Dynamic GGUF weights at 143.9 GB, with calibration and fidelity testing across coding, tool use and other workloads.
• @ViC305 — SAGE-EXL3, token-level fidelity measurements and a single-DGX-Spark recipe.
• @PeasantSmith — Project Maya quants and expert offloading for local coding and tool use.
• @MiaAI_lab — EXL3-EAQ quantization work.
• @jundotkim + mlx-community — oQ quants and DSpark-powered decoding through oMLX on Apple Silicon.
• @AIatAMD — Quark MXFP4 adapted for AMD Instinct.
• @atomic_chat_hq — GGUFs for local desktop workflows.
• @superalesha — custom inference work combining quantized weights, expert caching and system RAM on 4× RTX 3090.
Every shared quant, kernel, measurement and recipe gives the next builder a better starting point. Thank you.

"One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models"

Looped Transformers typically perform much worse than standard models when looping only once.

NVIDIA introduces Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), which uses gated state updates and trains with different loop counts simultaneously, allowing a single model to trade inference compute for accuracy without sacrificing its one-loop performance.

On a 4B model, one-loop accuracy comes within 0.52% of a standard Transformer, while four loops improve average accuracy by 7.25%. Its Koi-4B model also improves its estimated Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index from 18 to 29 by increasing loop count alone.

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

tweets.text:
Increasingly this will be the new job description for a lot of roles, not just coding. We’re clearly moving from a world where agents help us do our work incrementally better or faster, to us helping agents do their work.

This turns everyone in one of these positions to that of a manager of a team of agents, instead of an individual contributor with just some added leverage from AI. The biggest areas of impact will be information-heavy jobs, like coding, cybersecurity, legal work, biotech, engineering, and many other fields. 

And as a result, in these jobs your leverage will begin to be decoupled from the normal ratio of hours spent working to output generated. For essentially the history of knowledge work the main variable you had to play with was hours of work done (assuming fixed level talent/coordination/strategy). 

Now we’ve separated these variables because agents can parallelize work for us, to in theory execute as much as we need to pull off whatever goal we’re trying to accomplish. The people and organizations that discover this sooner, and orient their operations around it, will see compounding gains in their workflows.
